newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices creep up in a hesitant market.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices creep up in a hesitant market.

text.p: Oil prices crept up a little on Wednesday but showed little inclination to move out of a tight cocoon in the absence of fresh fundamental news, traders said.

World benchmark crude oil Brent Blend from the North Sea traded 12 cents higher at $22.55 a barrel in the afternoon after opening unchanged and holding in a tight range for much of the morning session.
Traders could not explain why the market was holding up after Tuesday's U.S. weekly oil stocks data was released by the American Petroleum Institute (API).

The figures showed a huge draw of 4.1 million barrels in weekly distillate stocks, which include heating oil. While the news would normally be bullish in the tail end of a winter market, a year-on-year comparison showed stocks were above year-ago levels for the first time since June 1995.

"Despite the big draw on distillates, the year-on-year comparison makes it a pretty bearish report. I'd sell heating oil on this news," said John Lichtblau, President of Petroleum Industry Research Foundation in New York.
"A few months ago, no one would have guessed that distillate stocks would be higher than a year ago. This was not expected, he added.

London futures for gas oil, used in Europe as heating fuel, reacted early to the API numbers and fell below the psychological $200 a tonne level for the first time in five months. February gas oil later recovered to trade $1.75 a tonne down at $201.25 a tonne.

"People are unsure after last night's API figures. The question on these figures is does the market move lower still or were the figures priced into last night's figures and therefore the market holds and maybe bounces back," a broker said.
Charles Gray of Prudential Bache Securities agreed, saying he was surprised the market fell on Tuesday ahead of publication of the API data.
"I guess you never sell a dull market," Gray said, adding that he expected the market to consolidate before moving on.

Low industry stocks in 1996 helped to push crude oil prices to a near six-year high of $25.06 a barrel in October after an anticipated growth in crude supply from producers outside the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) failed to materialise and Iraqi crude stayed off the market.
Mild spells of winter weather in the Northeast U.S. and Northwest European heating oil markets also have also taken the edge off prices for heating oil in recent weeks
